title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
Let’s start with the actual announcement.
A few weeks ago, Merck and Moderna released a clinical update that sent a jolt of genuine excitement through the oncology world:
If you don’t read clinical press releases for a living, that headline looks like a wall of biotech alphabet soup. But behind those acronyms is a genuinely historic milestone: for the first time in medical history, an individualized cancer vaccine—designed by computers specifically for each patient’s unique tumor—has succeeded in a definitive Phase 3 trial.
Before diving into how this incredible machine works, let’s translate what this news actually means in plain English.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: 1. The Real Danger: Stage IV and Metastasis
text:
1. The Real Danger: Stage IV and Metastasis
Melanoma is an aggressive form of skin cancer. When solid tumors are diagnosed, doctors assign them a stage from I to IV. You don’t need to memorize the intricacies of every intermediate stage, but here is the critical rule: Stage IV is the most dangerous stage in oncology.
Why? Because Stage IV means distant metastasis—the cancer cells have broken away from the skin, traveled through the bloodstream or lymphatic vessels, and colonized distant vital organs like the lungs, liver, bones, or brain. Once cancer metastasizes widely to vital organs, it becomes exponentially harder to treat and frequently fatal.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: 2. The Illusion of “Clean Margins” & Dormant Micrometastases
text:
2. The Illusion of “Clean Margins” & Dormant Micrometastases
When a patient has high-risk melanoma (Stages IIB through IV), a surgeon cuts out the visible tumor. If the pathology report comes back showing “complete surgical resection” with “clean margins,” it means the surgeon got all the cancer they could physically see.
Here is the catch: surgery rarely clears 100% of the cells.
Long before surgery, microscopic clusters of malignant cells—known as dormant micrometastases—often detach and drift invisibly into circulation. These clusters are far too small to show up on CT or PET scans. Left alone, they can sit quietly for months or even years, only to “wake up” later and seed deadly metastatic tumors.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
3. The Role of Adjuvant Therapy
This brings us to adjuvant therapy. Adjuvant treatment is therapy given after surgery to act as an insurance policy. Its sole job is to hunt down and eliminate those invisible dormant micrometastases before they can take root.
[Surgery: Primary Tumor Removed] ──> [Invisible Micrometastases Linger in Body]
                                                  │
                   ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
                   ▼                                                             ▼
       [Standard Adjuvant Care]                                    [Personalized Vaccine + Keytruda]
         Keytruda alone blocks                                      Keytruda unblocks the immune system 
        cancer's defense switches                                   WHILE custom mRNA directs T-cells
                                                                    to hunt specific tumor mutations

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: 4. The Trial Yardsticks: RFS vs. DMFS
text:
4. The Trial Yardsticks: RFS vs. DMFS
The Phase 3 trial (INTerpath-001) tested whether adding Moderna’s custom vaccine to Merck’s standard immunotherapy (Keytruda) could stop these micrometastases better than Keytruda alone:

Recurrence-Free Survival (RFS): Did the cancer stay away, or did it return locally or in nearby lymph nodes?
Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS): Did the cancer spread to distant vital organs like the lungs, liver, or brain?

The result? The combination met both endpoints with high statistical significance. Adding the custom mRNA vaccine significantly improved the odds of staying cancer-free and stopped the disease from spreading to distant organs compared to the world’s best standard-of-care drug.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: The Dual Mechanism: The Gas Pedal and the Brake
text:
The Dual Mechanism: The Gas Pedal and the Brake
To understand why this combination works, we first need to answer an obvious question: how does Keytruda work on its own when there is no mRNA vaccine?

How Keytruda Works Alone (Releasing Pre-Existing T-Cells)
Your immune system is not entirely blind to cancer. In many patients, a small squad of T-cells naturally stumbles upon the tumor, recognizes a mutated protein, and attempts to attack. These are known as Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs).
However, cancer cells quickly adapt. To defend themselves, tumors display a surface protein called PD-L1. When PD-L1 connects with the PD-1 receptor on an attacking T-cell, it acts as a molecular handbrake, flipping a biochemical “off-switch” that puts the T-cell into a state of exhaustion and paralysis. The T-cells are physically present at the tumor, but their weapons are locked.
Keytruda (pembrolizumab) is a monoclonal antibody that caps the PD-1 receptor on T-cells. By physically blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 connection, Keytruda prevents the cancer from engaging that off-switch. It releases the emergency brake, re-invigorating those exhausted, pre-existing T-cells so they can resume fighting.
How Keytruda Works Alone:
[Pre-existing, Exhausted T-Cells] ──(Keytruda Blocks PD-1)──> [T-Cells Re-awaken & Attack]
* Catch: Relies entirely on whatever random T-cells the patient happens to already have.


Why Keytruda Alone Hits a Ceiling
Keytruda revolutionized oncology, but on its own, it has a fundamental limitation: it relies on luck.
Keytruda cannot create new T-cells or choose what they target. It can only unchain the T-cells that the patient’s body has already generated naturally. If a patient has very few tumor-reactive T-cells, or if their natural T-cells are aimed at weak targets, releasing the brake achieves very little.
Furthermore, in the post-surgical (adjuvant) setting, the surgeon has already removed the primary tumor mass. Without a large tumor constantly stimulating the immune system, there are very few naturally active T-cells circulating to hunt down microscopic remnants.


Why the Personalized Vaccine Completes the Circuit
This is where Moderna’s mRNA vaccine transforms the equation:
Step 1: The Gas Pedal (Moderna mRNA Vaccine)
Does not rely on luck. Actively manufactures a brand-new, massive army 
of millions of T-cells trained specifically on up to 34 tumor mutations.

Step 2: Releasing the Brake (Keytruda Anti-PD-1)
Ensures that when these newly minted T-cells reach surviving cancer 
cells, the tumor cannot use PD-L1 to switch them off.

The mRNA Vaccine acts as the Gas Pedal: Instead of hoping the immune system notices the cancer, the vaccine delivers a clear intelligence briefing. It forces dendritic cells to present up to 34 mathematically optimized tumor neoantigens, triggering massive clonal expansion of fresh, high-affinity killer T-cells.
Keytruda acts as Releasing the Brake: As this newly trained army circulates to hunt down dormant micrometastases, Keytruda ensures the cancer’s PD-L1 shield cannot disarm them.

Giving Keytruda alone is like taking your foot off the brake in a car with an empty gas tank—the car is free to move, but there is no engine driving it forward. Giving the vaccine alone is like stepping on the gas with the emergency brake locked.
Used together, the vaccine builds and accelerates the engine, while Keytruda removes the brake.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: Why mRNA Beats DNA and Peptides
text:
Why mRNA Beats DNA and Peptides
To deliver up to 34 personalized targets within the 6-week surgical window, the choice of biological delivery vehicle is decisive:

Where It Operates

Synthetic peptides were the historical standard in experimental cancer vaccines. But synthesizing 34 distinct peptide chains for a single patient requires 34 separate chemical syntheses, purifications, and quality-control runs. Because peptides vary radically in solubility, charge, and chemical stability, batch failures across 34 simultaneous reactions make a 6-week turnaround impossible.
mRNA solved this by standardizing the physical chemistry.
Whether an mRNA strand codes for neoantigen A or neoantigen B, its chemical properties are virtually identical. The synthesis machinery, purification columns, and lipid nanoparticle formulation remain invariant. The factory operates like a digital compiler: the physical hardware stays the same, and only the digital sequence sent to the synthesizer changes.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: The Lock and Key: Mutations vs. HLA Diversity
text:
The Lock and Key: Mutations vs. HLA Diversity
Melanoma carries an enormous number of mutations caused by ultraviolet sun damage. A single biopsy typically reveals hundreds or thousands of DNA alterations.
However, a mutation deep inside a cancer cell is completely invisible to passing T-cells. For the immune system to see it, the cell must chop the mutated protein into short peptide fragments (8–11 amino acids long) and display them on surface presentation platters called Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) molecules (part of the Major Histocompatibility Complex, or MHC).
Here is the computational wall:

Extreme Genetic Diversity: HLA genes are the most polymorphic genes in the human genome, with tens of thousands of known allele variants across humanity.
The Unique Molecular Pocket: Every person inherits a unique combination of HLA alleles. Each HLA molecule forms a physical pocket with distinct chemical charges and anchor points.
Zero Transferability: A mutation that fits perfectly into Patient A’s HLA-A*02:01 pocket will be completely ignored by Patient B’s HLA-A*24:02 pocket.

You cannot manufacture an “off-the-shelf” melanoma vaccine because a target that cures one patient is invisible in another.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
The Needle in the Haystack
From that initial pool of ~1,000 mutations in a patient’s tumor:

Only 30–50% are actively transcribed into RNA at levels high enough to matter.
Less than 2% of those expressed peptides have the exact biochemical geometry to bind the patient’s specific HLA molecules and reach the outer cell surface.
Less than 20% of presented peptides look sufficiently “foreign” to stimulate a T-cell receptor rather than being dismissed as normal self-tissue.

Moderna’s vaccine construct has room for exactly 34 neoantigens.
If you pick the wrong 34, you inject a useless sequence while the patient’s cancer returns. In the past, validating candidate targets required isolating patient blood cells and testing peptides one by one in petri dishes—a process taking 6 to 12 months.
Instead of months of manual pipetting, cloud-based machine learning pipelines evaluate thousands of genetic variants in hours. Predictive neural networks model the intracellular processing pipeline, score which mutations will stably bind the patient’s specific HLA alleles, and compile the final 34-target sequence into a single optimized mRNA string.






NoteComing Soon in Part 2: Inside the Algorithmic Compiler



How does software turn raw genomic files into a life-saving molecular sequence? In a dedicated follow-up article, we will go deep inside the machine learning stack:

Parsing raw FASTQ sequencing reads and denoising machine artifacts.
How deep neural networks trained on mass-spectrometry immunopeptidomics predict HLA presentation.
TCR foreignness scoring to overcome central immune tolerance.
Generative mRNA design: optimizing cleavable linkers, codon adaptation (CAI), and secondary RNA folding to prevent ribosomal stalling.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
The Next Frontier: Scaling \(N=1\) Manufacturing
The computational models run in hours; the remaining industrial challenge is physical scaling.
Traditional pharmaceutical manufacturing is built around large-batch economy of scale: making thousands of identical doses in a single massive bioreactor. Individualized neoantigen therapy requires \(N=1\) manufacturing—thousands of unique, small-scale synthesis runs happening in parallel, each requiring strict sterility, zero cross-contamination, and rapid release testing.
Building automated, modular manufacturing facilities that can handle tens of thousands of individualized batches every year is the operational bridge between this clinical milestone and widespread worldwide access.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: 1. The Clinical Trial Evidence Base & Regulatory Path
text:
1. The Clinical Trial Evidence Base & Regulatory Path

The Pivotal Phase 3 Trial: INTerpath-001 (NCT05933577)

Trial Title: A Phase 3, Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo- and Active-Comparator-Controlled Study of Adjuvant V940 (mRNA-4157) Plus Pembrolizumab in Participants With Resected High-Risk (Stage IIB-IV) Melanoma.
Design: Enrolled ~1,089 patients across ~165 global clinical sites. Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive mRNA-4157 (1 mg IM every 3 weeks for up to 9 doses) plus pembrolizumab (200 mg IV every 3 weeks for up to 18 cycles) versus placebo plus pembrolizumab.
Significance: The first individualized neoantigen therapy in oncology history to hit primary and secondary endpoints in a definitive Phase 3 trial.
Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05933577

The Phase 2b Proof-of-Concept: KEYNOTE-942 (The Lancet, 2024)

Paper: Weber, J. S., et al. “Individualised neoantigen therapy mRNA-4157 (V940) plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone in resected melanoma (KEYNOTE-942): a randomised, open-label, phase 2b trial.” The Lancet, 2024; 403(10427): 632–644. DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)02268-7.
Key Data: 157 patients with resected Stage IIIB–IV melanoma. Adding the mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 44% (\(\text{Hazard Ratio [HR]} = 0.561; 95\%\text{ CI: } 0.309\text{--}1.017; p=0.053\)) and reduced the risk of distant metastasis or death by 65% (\(\text{HR} = 0.347; 95\%\text{ CI: } 0.145\text{--}0.828\)). Long-term follow-up presented at ASCO 2024 demonstrated durable 3-year recurrence-free survival benefits.

Regulatory Designations:

FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation (Feb 2023): Granted by the U.S. FDA to expedite the development and review of mRNA-4157 + Keytruda for adjuvant melanoma.
EMA Priority Medicines (PRIME) Scheme (Apr 2023): Granted by the European Medicines Agency to accelerate regulatory access across the EU.

The Expanding Clinical Pipeline:

INTerpath-002 (NCT06077760): Phase 3 randomized study evaluating adjuvant V940 + Keytruda in completely resected Stage II, IIIA, and IIIB Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC).
INTerpath-004 (NCT06295809): Phase 2 trial in muscle-invasive bladder cancer / urothelial carcinoma.
INTerpath-005 (NCT06307431): Phase 2 trial in advanced renal cell carcinoma (kidney cancer).
INTerpath-007 (NCT06295822): Phase 2 trial in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC).

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
section: 2. Seminal Research Papers: From Concept to Clinical Reality
text:
2. Seminal Research Papers: From Concept to Clinical Reality

The Neoantigen Paradigm:

Paper: Schumacher, T. N., & Schreiber, R. D. (2015). “Neoantigens in cancer immunotherapy.” Science, 348(6230), 69–74. DOI: 10.1126/science.aaa4971.
Why It Matters: The seminal paper establishing that cancer-specific somatic mutations create novel, foreign peptide flags (neoantigens) that are recognized by CD8+ and CD4+ T-cells without triggering central self-tolerance.

The First Personalized RNA Vaccines in Humans:

Paper: Sahin, U., et al. (2017). “Personalized RNA mutanome vaccines mobilize poly-specific therapeutic immunity against cancer.” Nature, 547(7662), 222–226. DOI: 10.1038/nature23003.
Why It Matters: Pioneering clinical proof-of-concept demonstrating that customized synthetic RNA encoding personalized somatic mutations induces de novo T-cell responses against multiple targets in advanced melanoma patients.

The Benchmark for Neoantigen Prediction Algorithms:

Paper: Wells, D. K., et al. (The TESLA Consortium) (2020). “Key Parameters of Tumor Epitope Immunogenicity Revealed by a Global Consortium for Cancer Immunotherapy.” Cell, 183(3), 818–834. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2020.09.015.
Why It Matters: A landmark global benchmark comparing neoantigen prediction pipelines across 36 academic and biotech groups. Proved that simple peptide-MHC binding affinity alone generates massive false-positive rates, demonstrating why multi-model pipelines incorporating proteasomal cleavage, RNA expression weighting, and mass spectrometry presentation are mandatory.

Mass-Spectrometry-Driven HLA Motif Modeling:

Paper: Sarkizova, S., et al. (2020). “A large peptidome dataset reveals HLA class I presentation rules and enables improved peptide-MHC prediction.” Nature Biotechnology, 38(2), 199–209. DOI: 10.1038/s41587-019-0322-9.
Why It Matters: Established the modern foundation for training deep neural networks directly on high-throughput mass spectrometry (\(LC\text{-}MS/MS\)) eluted ligand data across thousands of HLA alleles, radically improving presentation prediction accuracy over historical synthetic binding assays.

Molecular Mechanics of Checkpoint Blockade:

Paper: Ribas, A., & Wolchok, J. D. (2018). “Cancer immunotherapy using checkpoint blockade.” Science, 359(6382), 1350–1355. DOI: 10.1126/science.aar4060.
Why It Matters: Comprehensive review of how chronic tumor antigen stimulation drives T-cell exhaustion via the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway, and how monoclonal antibodies physically disengage this checkpoint brake.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
3. Key Concepts & Clinical Mechanics Glossary

Complete Surgical Resection (\(R_0\) Resection): Removal of all macroscopic tumor tissue with microscopic margins free of malignant cells. However, an \(R_0\) margin does not preclude the existence of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) or disseminated micrometastases in regional or distant tissue beds.
Dormant Micrometastases: Subclinical clusters of cancer cells that have detached from the primary lesion and lodged in distant organs. They frequently enter a state of cellular quiescence (\(G_0\) cell cycle arrest), evading standard imaging and conventional chemotherapies that target dividing cells, until microenvironmental cues reactivate malignant proliferation.
Adjuvant Therapy: Systemic treatment administered after complete surgical removal of primary disease, designed to sterilize occult micrometastatic disease and permanently prevent recurrence.
Recurrence-Free Survival (RFS): The time elapsed from surgical resection or study randomization until confirmed local, regional, or distant recurrence, or death from any cause.
Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS): The time elapsed until cancer colonizes distant organs (e.g., lungs, liver, brain, bone). In melanoma, DMFS is the single strongest clinical surrogate for Overall Survival (OS).
Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB): The number of non-synonymous somatic mutations per megabase (Mb) of sequenced tumor DNA. Melanoma carries one of the highest TMBs (\(>15 \text{ mutations/Mb}\)) due to ultraviolet-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer formation (\(C \rightarrow T\) transitions), providing a dense pool of neoantigen candidates.
Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) System: The human Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC). Polygenic and polymorphic cell-surface glycoproteins that bind peptide fragments (8–11 amino acids for Class I; 13–17 amino acids for Class II) and display them on the cell membrane for immune surveillance by T-cell receptors.
Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs): Endogenous host immune cells (predominantly CD8+ cytolytic and CD4+ helper T-cells) that have migrated into the tumor microenvironment.
Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs): Sub-100 nm synthetic spheres composed of ionizable lipids, structural phospholipids, cholesterol, and PEGylated lipids. LNPs protect synthetic mRNA from rapid enzymatic degradation by circulating ribonucleases and facilitate receptor-mediated endocytosis and endosomal escape into the cytoplasm.

title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
text:
4. Open-Access Computational Biology Databases & Tools
For engineers and computational biologists interested in exploring neoantigen prediction software:

Immune Epitope Database (IEDB): iedb.org — Free, NIAID-supported repository cataloging millions of experimentally validated epitopes, MHC binding measurements, and T-cell activation assays.
NetMHCpan 4.1 & NetMHCIIpan 4.0: services.healthtech.dtu.dk — Widely used pan-specific neural network tools predicting peptide binding across all known human HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DP/-DQ/-DR alleles.
MHCflurry 2.0: github.com/openvax/mhcflurry — Open-source deep learning framework integrating proteasomal antigen processing, TAP transport, and MHC Class I surface presentation predictors.
OpenVax Pipeline: github.com/openvax — An open-source suite of bioinformatics tools for variant calling, epitope prediction, and personalized vaccine design from paired tumor/normal FASTQ files.
UCSC Cancer Genomics Browser & TCGA: cancergenome.nih.gov — The Cancer Genome Atlas repository containing whole-exome sequencing and RNA-seq data across thousands of human tumors.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text: This chapter deals with attention mechanisms. At a very high level, the flow of the chapters is as follows:

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
section: 1.1 Better but slightly more compute-constrained approach
text:
1.1 Better but slightly more compute-constrained approach
Naturally, we should follow how human translators work: take input in the language, synthesize it, and then return the output in the target language. In a computational sense, this is what Encoder-Decoders are. The Encoder acts like the translator listening to the source sentence and forming a mental “summary” of the idea. This summary—technically called a context vector—is then passed to the Decoder, which begins speaking the sentence in the new language. Before Transformers, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) were the standard norm. RNNs are well-suited for sequential data because they process information one step at a time, feeding the output of the previous word into the current step to maintain a sense of history.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
1.2 Encoder-Decoder RNNs trouble
Once we move to encoder-decoder RNNs, the challenges are two-fold. As the input text is fed into the encoder, it processes it sequentially and updates its hidden state. It captures the entire meaning of the sentence in the final hidden state. The decoder then takes this “bottleneck” state to start generating the translation.
The big limitation is that RNNs can’t directly access earlier hidden states from the encoder during decoding. This leads to lost context.

The Translator’s Struggle: Imagine our translator is listening to a 50-word sentence. By the time the speaker finishes, the translator has a general “vibe” of the sentence, but they’ve likely forgotten the specific adjectives used at the very beginning. Because the RNN forces the entire meaning into one single vector, the “signal” from the start of the sequence washes out by the time it reaches the end.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
1.3 The Solution: Bahdanau Attention
The current solution is the Attention Mechanism, which captures these data dependencies. Instead of forcing the translator to rely on a single, fading memory of the whole sentence, the Bahdanau Attention mechanism allows the translator to “re-read” specific parts of the source text as they generate each word.
When the decoder is about to produce a word, it looks back at all the encoder’s hidden states and assigns a “weight” to them. If the translator is currently translating a noun, the attention mechanism tells them to “focus” more on the original noun and its modifiers in the source sentence, rather than the distant verbs.
Mathematically, the context vector for each decoding step is a weighted sum of all encoder hidden states : \[c_t = \sum_{i=1}^{T} \alpha_{ti} h_i\] Where \(\alpha_{ti}\) represents the “attention score,” or how much focus the translator is giving to word while producing word . This ensures that no matter how long the sequence is, the important details are never truly lost.

Let’s now jump on how the Attention mechanism works Attention mechanism is like the engine that drives the entire transformer block. Once we get a hang of the attention mechanism, the rest of the parts are relatively easy to fill in.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.1 Step 1
Generating intermediate weight W which is the dot product on the embedding vector for each token.


Code

   [0.57, 0.85, 0.64], # starts   (x^3)
   [0.22, 0.58, 0.33], # with     (x^4)
   [0.77, 0.25, 0.10], # one      (x^5)
   [0.05, 0.80, 0.55]] # step     (x^6)
)

# For demonstration purposes, we select one input token
query = inputs[1]

# 
attn_scores_2 = torch.empty(inputs.shape[0])
# print(attn_scores_2)

for i , x_i in enumerate(inputs):
    attn_scores_2[i] = torch.dot(x_i, query)


print(f"Attention score for second word i.e Journey {attn_scores_2}")


Just for more clarity, the dimension is equal to the number of tokens because the embeddding vector of the token ‘journey’ now has a dot product with all the tokens in the input text.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.2 Step 2:
Normalizing the intermediate weights now. The weight should sum up on a scale of 0 to 1. The easiest way to do this is using softmax layer.


Code
attn_weights_2 = torch.softmax(attn_scores_2, dim =0)
print(f"This is normalizing the vector of immediate weights {attn_weights_2}")
print(f"Sum should be 1: {attn_weights_2.sum()}")

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.3 Step 3:
A weighted sum of the embeddings vector and the normalized attention weight.


Code
query = inputs[1]
context_vec_2 = torch.zeros(query.shape)
for i, x_i in enumerate(inputs):
    context_vec_2 += attn_weights_2[i]*x_i
print(f"The final attention weight: {context_vec_2}")


The resultant vector for one token is the same as the input token embeddings size From a code perspective, this is a relatively poor. But for demonstration purposes, this will do.
When reviewing the code, an obvious question is the difference between torch.zeros vs torch.empty. THe way are pretty much the same.

Torch.zero initializes matrix of all zeros. The memory allocation for this is done. Torch.empty allocates memory but does not initialize it. This means that we should not use it with a sum operation. This means that if we print torch.empty it will return whatever is present in the memory allocation from before. The reason we use it is because it is slightly faster.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.4 Step 4:
So far, we have only done this for one token. Let’s extend this to the whole list of input tokens.


Code
attn_scores = torch.empty(inputs.shape)
print(attn_scores)
for i, x_i in enumerate(inputs):
    for j , x_j in enumerate(inputs):
        attn_scores[i] = torch.dot(x_i, x_j)
print(f"Attention score for all words {attn_scores}")


A slightly advanced approach leveraging linear algebra is:


Code
# Step 1
attn_scores = inputs @ inputs.T 

# Step 2
attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim =-1) # Do it on the last dimension of the vector, which in this case is equal to token size.

# Step 3

all_context_vectors = attn_weights @ inputs
print(all_context_vectors)


To summarize iteration 1, we did a watered down version of self attention. We took one token as an input, dot product across all tokens embeddings, normalize the resultant weights across token length and finally we do a sum proudct of this normalized weight with each embedding vector. We repeat the same exercise for all tokens. Few important things to consider for the scaled version. attn_scores has dimensions: token_length * token_length attn_weights: token_length * token_length all_context_vectors: token_length * embedding_size

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
2.5 Translator’s Learnings from this step
At this stage, our translator has stopped using a word-for-word dictionary. They’ve realized that words are defined by their neighbors. When they see the word “bank,” they now look at the rest of the sentence to see if there are words like “river” or “money.” They are building a rough ‘vibe’ of the sentence, but they’re still using a fixed set of rules and can’t yet adapt their focus based on the specific task at hand.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
3.1 Translator’s Learnings from this step
Now, the translator has learned that not all relationships are equal. By introducing \(W_q\), \(W_k\), and \(W_v\), they’ve developed three distinct mental frameworks: What am I looking for? (Query), What do I offer to others? (Key), and What is the actual meaning? (Value). They are no longer just looking at neighbors; they are actively learning which connections are the most important for understanding the “soul” of the sentence. There is one hack that the translator is using right now. It has a look up to future words.

title: Chapter 03: Coding Attention Mechanisms
text:
4.1 The steps are the following:

Calculate Attention scores
Apply SoftMax and get attention weights
Mask with 0 above the diagonal
Normalize the rows of the masked attention scores

Implementing this pretty much the same way as before. We will do small codes with one go, then we will formalize with a class


Code
# First two steps combined
queries = sa_v2.W_query(inputs)

keys = sa_v2.W_key(inputs)

attnn_scores = queries @ keys.T
attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores/ keys.shape[-1]** 0.5, dim = -1)

print(attn_weights)

# Third step - this looks a whole lot complex but is rather simple. If you only think about the values that tril is generating.
context_length = attn_scores.shape[0]
masked_simple = torch.tril(torch.ones(context_length,context_length))
print(masked_simple)

# Fourth step
row_sums = masked_simple.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
masked_simple_norm = masked_simple/row_sums
print(masked_simple_norm)


This is a pretty neat implementation which hits our objective of causal attention model right on the head. However, there is a room for a few improvements primarily from a mathematical standpoint. 1. Use negative infinity to get rid of that extra normalization at step 4. The whole idea of step 4 was normalize all the values left after zeroing upper traingle of the matrix.When we use negative infinity with softmax the output is 0 and 2. Dropouts addition to avoid overfitting - This is a technique where randomly selected hidden layer inputs are ignored during training. This avoids overfitting by making sure that the model does not rely heavily on a specific set of hidden layer inputs. Dropouts is only used during training and not inference.
We can combine all of this in one go and create our final class. We will also make it work with batches.


Code
batch = torch.stack((inputs,inputs), dim = 0)
print(batch.shape) ## The shape now must be 2 * 6 * 3 which is 2 items in the batch. 6 tokens in each batch. Each token with an embedding size of 3

class CausalAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, context_length, dropout, qkv_bias=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_out = d_out
        self.W_query = nn.Linear(d_in,d_out,bias = qkv_bias)
        self.W_key = nn.Linear(d_in,d_out,bias = qkv_bias)
        self.W_value = nn.Linear(d_in,d_out,bias = qkv_bias)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) # The input here indicates the percentage of values in the matrix that must be zero

        # This tells pytorch that these weights are non trainable so no gradient-descent for them. The mask is saved in state_dict and is loaded/saced with the model
        self.register_buffer(
            'mask',
            torch.triu(torch.ones(context_length,context_length),diagonal=1)
        ) # Will take this in a bit

    def forward(self, x):
        b, num_tokens, d_in = x.shape # This is the reason that we do not need to initialize the d_in. d_in is derived from an object of the class

        # Same step as the previous loop
        # Shape of x = 2,6,3
        # Shape of key, query, value is 2,6,2
        keys = self.W_key(x) 
        queries = self.W_query(x)
        values = self.W_value(x)

        # Pretty much the same as the previous step. This is just doing transformations so that keys merge properly.
        # Shape of attention scores is 2,6,6
        # Keys.transpose essentially means switching the 1st dimenion with the second. so the dimesion is now 2,2,6
        # queries (2,6,2) @ keys.transpose(1,2) (2,2,6) ==> (2,6,6)
        # this is because torch considers everythin after the last two dimesnions as batch. A better way to say this would be anything the matrix multipllication here is 6,2 @ 2,6 --> 6,6 and then there are two batches in each.

        attn_scores = queries @ keys.transpose(1,2)
        
        # This is making sure that all the values that are masked are now 
        # Fill elemts of the tensor with value where mask is true. The shape of the mask must be broadcastable
        attn_scores.masked_fill_(self.mask.bool()[:num_tokens, :num_tokens],-torch.inf)

        # This is the same step as before.
        attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores/keys.shape[-1]**0.5, dim = -1)

        # Droput we had discussed
        # Zeroes the values of the matrix at random. the shape of the matrix is the same

        attn_weights = self.dropout(attn_weights)

        # This the same step as before.
        # attn_weights dim = (2,6,6). values dim (2,6,2) --> 2,6,2
        context_vec = attn_weights @ values

        return context_vec


The wraps up Causal Attention. Causal attention is the base on which the multi- headed attention is based on. Causal Attention also known as masked attention is a specialized form of self-attention. It restricts a model to only review previous and current inputs in a sequence when processing any given token when computing attention scores.

text:
4.2 Translator’s Learnings from this step
Our translator is now writing a book. They’ve learned a vital rule: no spoilers. By masking the future, the translator forces themselves to generate the story one word at a time, using only what has been “said” so far. This discipline ensures the translation flows logically from start to finish, preventing the model from ‘cheating’ by looking at the end of the sentence before it has even started the beginning.

Finally, our single translator has become a full editorial team. One expert focuses on the tense of the verbs, another tracks the gender of the pronouns, and a third looks for poetic metaphors. By working in parallel, they catch nuances that a single mind would miss. They then sit down together (the final linear projection) to merge their individual notes into one perfect, polished masterpiece.

title: A Hopeful Guide to Navigating Spinal Injury: Our Family’s Experience at ISIC
text: My father has had two major surgeries in the neck at the Indian Spinal Injury Center, and both have been successful. But this post isn’t just about that. I want this post to give you hope that there is a hospital which could really help you in case you suffer from a spine injury. The world does not turn into a bleak place. Please treat this as a general playbook from one family to another, not as medical advice. Anything I mention that sounds like medical advice here should be discussed with your own doctors.

title: A Hopeful Guide to Navigating Spinal Injury: Our Family’s Experience at ISIC
text:
The main leverage is time
Time is of the essence when dealing with spinal injuries. The progression of these injuries is rapid and can lead to significant deterioration within a short period, often no more than 10 days to reach a critical stage. Spinal injuries follow an almost exponential curve of decline if not addressed promptly.
Initial symptoms may include a loss of balance, followed by numbness in the fingers and legs. This can then progress to a lack of coordination in the legs, causing a limping gait. In advanced stages, individuals may lose motor functions and control over bladder and bowel movements, leading to a profound loss of confidence. My father experienced this severe stage during his first spinal injury.
Fortunately, we were able to intervene earlier during his second injury. It is crucial to understand that this deterioration can occur within 1 to 3 days. A fall can significantly accelerate this process. Therefore, it is vital not to underestimate the severity of these injuries and to prevent misdiagnosis. My father’s initial symptoms were mistakenly attributed to diabetes.

title: A Hopeful Guide to Navigating Spinal Injury: Our Family’s Experience at ISIC
section: We are in the same boat you and I
text:
We are in the same boat you and I
Indian Healthcare for all its pros and cons is working like an engine. There are great hospitals near Delhi which are semi private. ISIC is one of them. You could go to AIMS for spinal injuries. But I would suggest against that. The reason is the backlog that AIMS has. No doubt, AIMS is the most affordable. It has probably the best doctors from India. But I think ISIC does a reasonable job of maintaining the balance between cost and good service. I don’t want to delve into past laurels because they are pretty much useless when it comes to the present day running of the hospital but ISIC runs smoothly. If you have Insurance they will be happy to take you in. I did not deal in cash but cash processing is also smooth judging by the queue.

title: A Hopeful Guide to Navigating Spinal Injury: Our Family’s Experience at ISIC
text:
Overcoming the surgery
One of the best things about this hospital is its rehabilitation unit. It is where the post-operative care happens, and this is not treated as an add-on; it is considered part of the treatment. All of the people I interacted with were very patient with patients. They would answer all your questions. My father was able to walk after 2 months of the surgery. I consider this to be a miracle of sorts. I think the hospital staff does a lot of things really well, but there is little being done to ensure transparency between departments. The doctors are transparent, but they do not always help the nursing staff explain their decisions. This leads to confusion for the attendants. The ICU times are perfect and do not need change. The hospital even gave me some slack for feeding my father without the nurse, which I am incredibly grateful for. Insurance paperwork is really a pain and there are 6 desks to visit. For an attendant, it may seem overwhelming. It is streamlined and people are really helpful, but from day 1, the paperwork seems like a lot. My only benchmark is Max Gurgaon near the Huda Metro Station where the paperwork is just a few signatures. But the positive is everyone tries to help. The staff in the Admissions office help you even if they are non-chalant

title: A Hopeful Guide to Navigating Spinal Injury: Our Family’s Experience at ISIC
text:
A practical guide to attendants

Coffee at the main cafeteria is expensive. Go to the retail store and they will sell you the same coffee for cheap. I needed a lot of coffee.
Junior doctors are your friends. Please listen to them
Guards are better in the night than during the day
Have good relations with the nurses, they do more paperwork in a day than what you do in a year. They will help you when you need it. Don’t ask for your test results from them because the doctor is supposed to inform you of that. If the doctors become of aware of this, nurses get a stick from the head nurse
Whatever games you are thinking that the hospital is playing to increase your bills, it is not

HDU is a High Dependency Unit. This is confusing to a lot of the patients. This means that the patient is out of danger but still needs active monitoring. The timings of visit are different from ICU. But rules are the same as the ICU. The doctor is there during visiting times to give you updates.
Do not get nurses in trouble with the doctors
Floor managers are there for assessing the arrangements. Please do not use them to get your way because they are the admin
If you are the sole attendant and there is no place to sleep, the best place is your car or near the emergency beside the Cafe Coffee Day. Do not go the attendant’s ward because that place is likely to be filled and is a den of mosquitos

Create a Culture: Designing a deliberate culture sets you up for the long term.
It is one thing to look into a foggy future with acuity and chart the course corrections that a company must make, but quite another to persuade employees, who might not see the changes ahead, to line up and work cooperatively to take the company in a new direction. For organizations, this alignment depends on two separate dimensions: 1. The extent to which members of the organization agree on what they want from their participation in the enterprise. 2. The extent to which they agree on which actions will produce the desired results.

Critical Takeaways

Avoid the marginal costs mistake: It is easier to hold to your principles 100% of the time than it is to hold to them 98% of the time.
Remember the importance of humility: The most humble people generally have a high level of self-esteem. They know who they are and they feel good about who they are. Humility is not defined by self-deprecating behavior or attitudes, but by the esteem with which a person regards others. True humbleness unlocks the opportunity to learn a lot from everyone around you.
Choosing the right yardstick: In the end, resolve to measure your life by the individuals you have touched and the people you have helped become better. ## Personal Note: What stood out most to me was the idea of intentionally creating a culture, especially the parallel between organizational culture and a family’s own culture at home. The article’s strongest takeaways for me were the importance of avoiding the marginal cost mistake and practicing humility in its truest sense.

Part 2: The Core Questions for an Excellent Life
To build a life of excellence, you must deeply understand the answers to these five questions: 1. What are my strengths? (Discovered via feedback analysis) 2. How do I work? - Do you process information best by reading or by listening/discussing? - Do you accomplish more working with others, or working alone? - Do you perform best as a decision-maker, or as an advisor on key matters? - Do you thrive under stress, or do you function optimally in a highly predictable environment? 3. What are my values? - What are your ethics and your most important responsibilities for living a worthy life? - Note: If your organization’s ethics do not resonate with your own values, your career will likely be marked by frustration and poor performance. 4. Where do I belong? - Combine your strengths, work style, and values to find the right environment. Fitting into the right environment transforms you from an acceptable employee into a star performer. 5. What can I contribute? - Instead of waiting to be told what to do, look at what the situation requires and decide how you can make the greatest organizational impact based on your strengths, style, and values.

Part 3: Responsibility for Relationships
Achieving anything meaningful requires working effectively with others. Managing yourself means taking full responsibility for relationships, which consists of two parts: - Accepting Individual Differences: Accept that your co-workers are individuals who will insist on behaving like human beings. They have their own strengths, values, and ways of getting things done. To be effective, you must learn and respect how they work. - Taking Responsibility for Communication: Most personality clashes in organizations happen because people do not know what others are doing, how they do it, or what results they expect. The remedy is simple: you must communicate and ask — ## Part 4: Managing the Second Half of Your Life As careers elongate, the “second half” of life (spanning 20 to 25 years) requires preparation long before you actually enter it. By the time many executives reach a stable point in their careers or stop climbing the corporate ladder, they need a secondary source of fulfillment. Developing this early ensures you can navigate major setbacks and keep growing. ### Three Ways to Introduce a Second Career 1. Moving Organizations: This involves taking a second career by simply moving from one type of organization to another. 2. Developing a Parallel Career: Staying in your primary job (full-time, part-time, or consulting) while simultaneously creating or joining a non-profit organization. 3. Social Entrepreneurship: For those who have been highly successful in their first jobs and choose to pivot into social entrepreneurship, continuing to use their lifelong skills but shifting their primary focus toward social impact. There are two ways to prepare for the second half of your life—actually, there are three. The first one is nothing more than moving from one kind of organization to another. This is practically taking a second career. The second way to prepare for the second half of life is to develop a parallel career. Many people who are very successful in the first half stay in the work they have been doing, either on a full-time or part-time or consulting basis, but in addition, they create or join a non-profit organization. The third kind of people are those who have been very successful in their first jobs, and that’s when they decide that they want to enter social entrepreneurship, doing what they have been doing all along, but spending less time on it.

Re-Inventing the Professional Self: Reflections on Managing Oneself in the Era of AI
I have often approached personal growth with the urgency of a 90-day sprint. When I previously tracked my decisions, I expected clear patterns and definitive results within three months, which led to frustration when progress was not obvious. Reading this reshaped that perspective. Realizing that feedback analysis is a steady 2-to-3-year discipline gave me permission to shift from chasing instant validation to committing to a longer practice of tracking my strengths, noticing where intellectual arrogance creates blind spots, and identifying where I truly excel. ### The Evolution of a Software Career in the AI Age From early on, and later in college, my path toward software became clear. Even then, however, I carried a quiet belief that I would not do software forever. I always sensed the need for a second act—some future space to step back, reflect, and pivot. Today, that instinct feels especially relevant. As AI rapidly changes the landscape for knowledge workers, waiting until the literal “second half of life” to reinvent oneself no longer feels realistic. AI is not only changing tools; it is accelerating the need to think seriously about alternate or parallel careers much earlier than previous generations did. This article reinforced for me that reinvention is not a reckless gamble but a recurring pattern in professional life. People have done this before. For me, developing a parallel career—perhaps in the non-profit or social entrepreneurship space while continuing to work in tech—is not merely a hedge against AI automation. It is a practical way to continue growing, learning, and staying relevant. ### Navigating Work Style: Readers vs. Listeners One of my most meaningful takeaways was the distinction between readers and listeners. It felt like a subtle but profound behavioral truth. Understanding whether someone processes the world best through written material or through discussion has a major impact on how that person should position themselves. It also helps explain why some environments feel natural while others feel draining, and why performance under pressure can vary so much. ### The Missing Piece: Responsibility for Relationships Looking back on my career so far, the section on responsibility for relationships resonated deeply. Accepting Individual Differences: Internalizing that coworkers are individuals who will insist on being human, each with their own strengths, values, and ways of getting things done. 2. title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
This post is about how agents work. The idea came from a blog post I was reading from Tidy Design Principles — the motivation is straightforward: cover everything you need to know to build an agent, from first principles. To keep the scope manageable, I will not touch upon how inference itself happens. That is a topic for another day.
Before we can talk about agents, we need to understand what they are built on top of: LLMs. So we will trace the evolution of LLMs — from a simple Q&A bot all the way to systems with agentic capabilities — and layer in the other concepts (tools, harnesses, caching) along the way.
Here is the roadmap:

LLMs as a Q&A bot — the stateless HTTP foundation
Multi-turn conversations — how context is maintained
System prompts — who sets the model’s behaviour
Client-side control — forking, structured output, and why you are in charge
Caching — why it is expensive
Tool calls — giving the LLM access to functions
The harness — who actually executes those tools
What is an agent? — tying it all together

The Q&A bot is the foundation everything else builds on, so we will spend the most time there.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
The HTTP foundation: statelessness
The first principle to grasp is that HTTP is stateless. Every request from the client to the server is a fresh, self-contained transaction. Once the server responds, it forgets everything about you.
This has a profound implication for LLM APIs: one question can only be answered in the context of a single request. The moment that transaction completes, the server retains no memory of your prior Q&A. The next time you send a message, the server starts from scratch.

Modern LLM platforms now have session and state management layers on top, but we are not concerned with those here. We care about the core capability of the LLM API itself, and that core is stateless.

This single fact — statelessness — is the thread that explains almost every “advanced” concept that follows.
This is a trimmed version of how the API works. There is a lot that goes on and is beyond the scope of the blog.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
Forking
At any point in a multi-turn conversation, you can fork: take the current message list, branch off, and start a parallel conversation from that point. You can run multiple branches simultaneously and pick the one that produced the best results. You can even jump back to an earlier turn and continue from there, ignoring later messages.
The LLM has no say in this. It simply processes whatever list you hand it.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
Structured output
You can ask the LLM to return its answer in a specific format — say, a JSON object with particular fields. This does not change the underlying mechanism. The response is still JSON, still part of the same message list, still resent on the next turn. Structured output is just a cleaner contract on top of the existing JSON interaction.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
The takeaway
What you send to the LLM at any given point — the system message, the assistant messages, the user messages, which turns to include or skip — is entirely controlled by the client. This is not a limitation; it is a superpower.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
text:
What the harness actually does
The description above makes the harness sound like a simple pass-through. In practice, the harness is doing a surprising amount of work at each step:
Argument validation. The LLM might return arguments that are malformed, missing required fields, or of the wrong type. The harness validates the tool-call request before executing anything. If the LLM calls get_today_date(format="dd-mm-yyyy") but your function does not accept a format parameter, the harness catches that and returns an error message to the LLM — not a crash.
Execution. The harness calls the actual function. This could be a local Python function, an HTTP call to an external API, a database query, or a shell command. The harness is agnostic to what the tool does — it just needs to run it and capture the return value.
Error handling. What happens if the function raises an exception? If the external API is down? If the database times out? The harness must catch these failures, format them as readable error messages, and feed them back to the LLM. The LLM can then decide to retry, try a different tool, or tell the user that something went wrong. Without the harness handling errors gracefully, a single API timeout would kill the entire conversation.
Serialisation. The function might return a Python object, a pandas DataFrame, a list of dicts, or raw bytes. The harness must serialise that into a string (or a JSON string) that the LLM can read. If the result is too large — say, a database query returning 10,000 rows — the harness must truncate, summarise, or paginate it. The LLM cannot digest raw binary or arbitrarily large payloads.
Logging and observability. In production, you want to know which tools were called, with what arguments, how long they took, and what they returned. The harness is the natural place to log all of this. This is not optional — when an agent misbehaves, the harness logs are how you debug it.
Security and permissions. The harness is the enforcement point. If a tool can delete files or make payments, the harness is where you add confirmation prompts, rate limits, or permission checks. The LLM should never have direct access to destructive operations — the harness mediates everything.

title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
section: What separates a toy agent from a production agent
text:
What separates a toy agent from a production agent
The loop above is deceptively simple. In practice, production agents add several layers on top:
Planning. Instead of blindly calling tools one at a time, a good agent first generates a plan. It breaks the user’s goal into sub-tasks and works through them deliberately. This is not magic — the “plan” is just the LLM producing a structured list of steps in its response, which the agent then follows.
State tracking (to-do lists). As the agent works through a multi-step task, it needs to track what it has done and what remains. A common pattern: the LLM generates a to-do list at the start, updates it after each step (marking items complete, adding new ones as it discovers them), and uses it to decide what to do next. This is exactly how Claude Code operates — you can watch it generate and update a checklist as it works.
Termination conditions. The while True loop needs an exit condition. Options include: the LLM explicitly says “I am done” (returns a response with no tool call), a maximum number of iterations is reached (to prevent infinite loops), or a token/time budget is exhausted. Getting this right is critical — an agent that never terminates is a bug, not a feature.
Human-in-the-loop checkpoints. For high-stakes actions (deploying code, making a payment, deleting files), the agent should pause and ask the user for confirmation before the harness executes the tool. Claude Code does this in its plan mode — it presents what it intends to do, asks for approval, and only then proceeds to execute.
Error recovery. When a tool call fails (API timeout, permission denied, invalid input), a production agent does not just crash. The LLM reads the error message, reasons about what went wrong, and tries an alternative approach — a different tool, different arguments, or asking the user for help.
